h: Battlefields, monuments and the Old Town
p: The castle is cared for by Historic Environment Scotland, and it pays to give it a good three hours or more. Costumed characters often bring the place to life, and the views from the ramparts help everything you've just learned click into place, because you can actually see the landscape that made this castle so important.

Before you head in, stop on the esplanade to see the statue of Robert the Bruce looking out over the land he fought for. From up here, look across the valley to the Wallace Monument on the Abbey Craig, built to honour William Wallace and his victory at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297. You can visit the monument too, and climbing its spiral staircase earns you another cracking view.

Bruce's own big moment came at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314, just south of the city. The Battle of Bannockburn visitor centre, run by the National Trust for Scotland, tells the story and is an easy add-on for anyone who's caught the history bug.

Don't skip Stirling's Old Town on the walk up or down. The streets are steep and cobbled, so sensible shoes are a must, but they're full of character. The Church of the Holy Rude, just below the castle, is where the infant James VI was crowned in 1567, and Argyll's Lodging is a fine 17th-century townhouse nearby. Below the Old Town, the modern city centre has shops, cafés and places to eat, and the railway station makes Stirling an easy day trip from both Edinburgh and Glasgow.
